mainEntity.name: Is it common to be truly allergic to dental local anaesthetic?

acceptedAnswer.text: True, confirmed allergic reactions to amide-type local anaesthetics — the type most commonly used in modern dentistry — are relatively uncommon. Many reactions that patients describe as allergies are more likely related to the adrenaline component, preservatives in the solution, anxiety, or a vasovagal (fainting) response. However, genuine allergies do occur and should always be properly investigated. If you have had a previous adverse reaction, your dentist will take this seriously and assess it thoroughly before recommending any treatment.

mainEntity.name: Can I still have dental implants if I have had a bad reaction to local anaesthetic?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes — but this depends entirely on the nature of your previous reaction and the outcome of a clinical assessment. If your reaction was related to a specific component of the anaesthetic rather than the anaesthetic agent itself, alternatives may be available. Sedation options may also be considered. Your dental clinician, potentially in liaison with an allergy specialist, will determine an appropriate and safe approach for your individual situation.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a local anaesthetic sensitivity and a true allergy?

acceptedAnswer.text: A sensitivity or adverse reaction may not involve the immune system. Symptoms such as palpitations, sweating, dizziness, or a racing heart are commonly caused by the adrenaline (epinephrine) component used in many dental anaesthetics rather than an allergic response. A true allergy involves an immune system reaction, potentially including hives, facial swelling, breathing difficulties, or anaphylaxis. These are far less common. A proper clinical and, where necessary, specialist allergy assessment can help distinguish between the two.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I need dental treatment but cannot have any local anaesthetic?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is a scenario that requires careful specialist input. In cases where a patient cannot safely receive standard local anaesthetics, a dental team may explore preservative-free alternatives, conscious IV sedation, or — in very exceptional cases — general anaesthesia in an appropriate clinical setting. No responsible dentist will proceed with treatment without a safe plan in place. Each case is assessed individually, and the safety of the patient is always the primary concern.

mainEntity.name: Will my dentist ask me about previous anaesthetic reactions before starting implant treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — a thorough medical history, including any previous adverse reactions to medications or anaesthetics, is a standard and essential part of any dental consultation, particularly before a surgical procedure such as implant placement. You should expect your dental team to ask detailed questions about any previous reactions, and it is important to provide as much information as possible to allow them to plan your care safely and appropriately.

mainEntity.name: Should I see my GP before visiting a dentist about this concern?

acceptedAnswer.text: It may be helpful, particularly if your GP has documentation of a previous reaction or has previously referred you to an allergist. However, you do not necessarily need to see your GP first — your dental team is well-placed to review your history and refer you onward if specialist allergy testing is considered necessary. Bringing any relevant medical correspondence to your dental consultation is always beneficial.
